strengths: Simple, intuitive idea: reconstructing optimization pairs from a problem-oriented perspective (across different users solving the same problem) rather than user-oriented (same user's iterative submissions), which is well-motivated by the observation that same-user iterations tend to be local tweaks while cross-user comparisons capture algorithmic innovation.

The core claim is supported by a reasonably careful qualitative/quantitative analysis (GPT-4 + human categorization of optimization types in Figure 3), showing PIE-Problem pairs are dominated by global algorithmic changes vs. PIE-User pairs.

Extensive experiments across multiple Code LLMs (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B) and decoding strategies (BEST@1, BEST@8), plus comparison against prompting baselines (Instruct, CoT, GPT-3.5/GPT-4).

Identification of a clear performance bottleneck (correctness) under PIE-Problem fine-tuning, and a reasonably thorough investigation of mitigation strategies (self-correct, curriculum learning, model merging), with model merging showing consistent improvements.
Additional analyses are provided: merge weight sensitivity (Figure 5), error analysis (Table 4), and illustrative qualitative examples (Figures 8-10) that support the narrative.
Dataset, code, and evaluation scripts promised to be released, aiding reproducibility.
Rigorous execution time measurement via gem5 simulator for deterministic and reproducible benchmarking.
weaknesses: The core contribution is primarily a data reconstruction/curation strategy rather than a novel modeling or algorithmic technique; the technical novelty is relatively limited (reordering/filtering existing PIE data by problem instead of by user, plus applying off-the-shelf model merging methods).

PIE-Problem dataset is much smaller than PIE-User (14,051 vs 56,086 training pairs, only 336 unique problems) and uses a strict 90% relative-time-improvement threshold; it's unclear how sensitive results are to this specific threshold choice, and no ablation is provided on threshold value or on matching training data size/budget between PIE-User and PIE-Problem for a fairer comparison.

The GPT-4-based categorization of optimization types (Figure 3) is somewhat circular evidence — using an LLM to judge whether optimizations are 'global' vs 'local' to validate a paper's central claim about global vs local optimization is a weak form of validation, especially given the paper itself notes GPT-4 over-classifies 'global' when changes are large; the human-annotated results (100 pairs) are quite small in sample size for a central claim.

The model merging method (linear/SLERP merge of two fine-tuned checkpoints) is an existing technique (Wortsman et al. 2022) applied fairly directly; the novelty of this section is limited to empirical application, and the mechanistic explanation of why merging works ("avoids fixed thinking patterns") is speculative rather than rigorously analyzed.

No comparison to more recent or stronger baselines such as retrieval-augmented approaches, dedicated program-repair-based self-correction, or larger/more capable general-purpose code models (e.g., GPT-4 fine-tuned, if accessible, or open strong coder models beyond CodeLlama/DeepSeek-Coder which are now somewhat dated).

The paper's narrative around "iterative vs innovative" makes a strong dichotomy, but the actual dataset construction and results show that problem-oriented pairs trade quantity/coverage for quality, and the correctness bottleneck significantly undermines the raw %OPT gains (i.e., without model merge, correctness drops substantially, e.g. from 91% to 72.5% for DeepSeek 33B at BEST@8), which tempers the headline claims in the abstract.

Limited discussion of computational cost and practicality of maintaining/curating a problem-oriented dataset at scale beyond competitive programming (CodeNet), and no discussion of generalization to broader real-world software engineering optimization tasks (the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this narrow scope).

The writing has some clarity issues (e.g., minor typos, dense notation in Section 3) and the related work section is somewhat thin, missing deeper discussion of alternative code-optimization approaches or recent works closer to this topic (e.g. superoptimization, other LLM-based performance optimization papers post-PIE).

strengths: The core motivation is intuitive and well illustrated: constructing optimization pairs from a single programmer's iterative history biases the model toward local/incremental edits, while pairing across different programmers on the same problem can expose genuinely different algorithmic strategies. The qualitative examples (Figures 2, 8-10) are convincing illustrations of this phenomenon.

The empirical results show a large, consistent improvement in %OPT and Speedup when switching from PIE-User to PIE-Problem fine-tuning across multiple model families and scales, which is at least suggestive that the reorganized pairs carry useful signal.
The paper is reasonably well organized, with clear metrics (using gem5 for deterministic timing) and a reasonably thorough breakdown of error types and merge-weight sensitivity.
Releasing the dataset/code (if it materializes) would be useful to the community given the sparse research on LLM-based performance optimization.
weaknesses: The central comparison between PIE-User and PIE-Problem is confounded by construction: PIE-Problem pairs are filtered to keep only pairs with >90% relative time improvement, while PIE-User pairs only need >10%. This means PIE-Problem is trained almost exclusively on dramatic, often algorithm-class-changing rewrites, which trivially explains higher %OPT/Speedup and also explains the large drop in correctness (the model is essentially being asked to imitate much more aggressive, harder-to-verify transformations). The paper never ablates this threshold or reports PIE-User results under a matched 90% threshold, so the 'problem-oriented vs user-oriented' framing is not isolated from the 'threshold' variable, undermining the paper's main causal claim.

The GPT-4-based categorization of 'global vs local' optimizations (used as key supporting evidence in Section 3) is self-referential and admittedly unreliable—the authors note GPT-4 over-classifies changes as 'global,' yet still lean on this analysis, with only 100 human-annotated pairs as a weak secondary check.

The PIE-Problem dataset is drastically smaller (336 unique problems / 14k pairs vs. 1,135 problems / 56k pairs), raising concerns about overfitting, statistical robustness, and whether gains generalize beyond the specific held-out problem distribution, especially since problems are selected precisely because they admit a huge speedup trajectory (a systematic, non-random subset of competitive-programming problems).

The correctness bottleneck identified (Table 2) is a serious issue that is only partially addressed: model merging recovers some correctness but final %OPT/Correct values (e.g., 76.65%/78.76% for the best merged model) still leave a large fraction of outputs unusable, and the method to fix this (naive linear/SLERP merging with a hand-tuned scalar weight) is not novel—it is a direct application of existing model-soup techniques with limited methodological contribution.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported for any of the headline numbers, despite the merge-weight curve (Figure 5) showing non-trivial sensitivity to a single hyperparameter (λ), which is only tuned/validated on the same test-adjacent setup without a clear held-out selection procedure.

The model pool is limited to CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder (up to 33B/34B); there is no fine-tuning experiment with more recent/stronger open code models, and GPT-4/GPT-3.5 are only evaluated via prompting, not fine-tuning, making the comparison between 'prompted state-of-the-art' and 'fine-tuned older models' somewhat apples-to-oranges when drawing conclusions about the value of problem-oriented data.

Curriculum learning and self-correction baselines are relatively weak/underexplored (single simple recipe each), so the claim that model merging is uniquely suited to reconcile the two data regimes is not rigorously established against stronger alternative baselines (e.g., mixed-data fine-tuning, weighted joint training, or multi-task objectives).

The contribution is largely a data-engineering repackaging of an existing dataset (PIE) plus a well-known model-merging technique; there is limited new methodological or algorithmic insight, and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges the scope is narrow (time-only optimization, given-code setting).

strengths: The central idea—shifting from user-oriented (same-programmer iterative) to problem-oriented (cross-programmer) optimization pairs—is intuitive, well-motivated with concrete illustrative examples (Figs. 2, 8-10), and addresses a real limitation of the PIE dataset.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five Code LLMs (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B) and multiple settings (instruct, CoT, PIE-User fine-tuning, PIE-Problem fine-tuning), with consistent and often large improvements in %OPT and Speedup.

The identification of a correctness bottleneck specific to problem-oriented fine-tuning, and the use of model merging (Linear/SLERP) to mitigate it, is a sensible and empirically validated follow-up contribution, with a clear best result (76.65% OPT, 5.09x speedup).

Useful ablations: merge-weight sweep (Fig. 5), comparison against self-correct and curriculum-learning baselines, and a detailed error analysis (Table 4) that meaningfully informs future work (e.g., program repair integration).

Reasonably rigorous evaluation methodology using gem5 simulation for deterministic timing measurements rather than noisy wall-clock time, and careful train/val/test problem-level separation to avoid leakage.
Dataset, code, and evaluation scripts are stated to be released, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: A significant methodological confound: PIE-Problem pairs are filtered to retain only >90% relative time improvement, whereas PIE-User pairs only require >10% improvement. This asymmetric filtering means PIE-Problem pairs are inherently easier/larger magnitude examples for the model to learn from, which could largely explain the performance gap rather than the 'problem-oriented' framing itself; no controlled ablation isolates the effect of interleaving-users vs. the effect of the stricter improvement threshold.

The core technical contribution is primarily a data curation/re-pairing strategy plus off-the-shelf application of existing model-merging methods (Wortsman et al., SLERP); limited methodological novelty for the model-merging portion.

The correctness bottleneck under PIE-Problem fine-tuning is a serious issue only partially addressed—model merging improves it but does not fully close the gap, and the underlying cause (why global optimization hurts correctness) is not deeply analyzed beyond high-level speculation.

The GPT-4-based categorization of 'global vs. local' optimization types (Fig. 3) is acknowledged to be biased (GPT-4 over-labels 'global'), and the human-verified subset is small (100 pairs), limiting confidence in the quantitative optimization-type statistics that motivate the paper's core claim.

Baseline models are somewhat dated (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder v1, GPT-3.5/4); no comparison with more recent or stronger open code models, nor with other performance-optimization-specific systems beyond PIE.

Limited to C++/competitive programming problems from a single source (CodeNet-derived); generalizability to other languages, real-world codebases, or other optimization objectives (memory, energy) is untested (acknowledged as limitation but not empirically explored).

No variance/significance reporting across multiple training runs or seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported gains are robust versus training noise, especially given relatively small PIE-Problem train set (14k pairs).

strengths: The core idea—reconstructing optimization pairs from a problem-oriented (cross-user) perspective rather than a user-oriented one—is simple, intuitive, and clearly motivated by the observation that single-programmer iterative refinement tends to be locally incremental.

The paper backs its central claim with a genuinely multi-faceted analysis: Control-Flow-Graph edit distance (structural), CodeT5+ embedding t-SNE (semantic), and both human and LLM sampling classification of optimization types, all pointing consistently to more global/algorithmic changes in PCO vs PIE.

Experimental gains are large and consistent across multiple model families and scales (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen2.5-Coder at 7B-33B), improving %OPT, speedup, and correctness substantially over PIE-based fine-tuning.

The anchor verification mechanism is a sensible, well-motivated design that exploits a genuine asymmetry in code optimization (the slow code is functionally correct and can serve as an oracle), and is compared against reasonable alternative refinement strategies (self-debugging, direct test generation) across three different backbone LLMs.
Extra analyses such as the PCO percentage/data-efficiency study and PIE-based ablation for anchor verification (Appendix G) add useful robustness evidence.
Reasonably strong reproducibility support: detailed prompts, training hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and multiple qualitative case studies are provided in appendices.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat limited: the problem-oriented construction is essentially a re-sorting/regrouping of existing submissions by runtime, and anchor verification is a straightforward application of using existing slow code as an oracle for test generation; neither involves substantial new modeling or algorithmic contribution.

The fairness protocol for comparing PIE and PCO (selecting PCO pairs with 'top speedup rankings' to match PIE pair counts) could bias the PCO dataset toward cleaner/higher-quality, more separable optimization pairs, potentially inflating the apparent advantage of the problem-oriented perspective independent of the perspective itself.

Cross-user runtime comparisons underlying PCO pair construction may be noisy (different submission times, potentially different judging environments/compilers), and pairing solutions from different programmers with very different logic as 'optimization pairs' is a stronger assumption than same-user iterative refinement; this validity concern is not empirically addressed (e.g., no analysis of how many 'optimized' pairs are actually semantically/functionally comparable beyond passing test cases).

The anchor verification mechanism's correctness gains are validated using the mechanism's own self-generated test cases (LLM-explained + generated inputs, executed on slow code); since these tests are not independently verified against a ground-truth test suite, the reported 'correctness' improvements might partly reflect overfitting to a weak, self-generated test suite rather than true functional correctness.

Only a single iteration of refinement is used for all compared methods (max iteration = 1), which limits the generality of conclusions about the anchor verification framework's benefits under more realistic iterative refinement budgets.

Baselines for the anchor verification comparison (self-debugging, direct test generation) are relatively simple re-implementations rather than strong established baselines from the literature (e.g., no comparison against more sophisticated test-based code repair/search methods), weakening the strength of the comparative claims.

No variance/statistical significance analysis is reported for the fine-tuning or refinement experiments (single run per configuration), which is a concern given the complexity of the pipeline and stochastic sampling (BEST@k, temperature 0.7).

Evaluation is confined entirely to competitive-programming style C++ code (CodeNet-derived), which may limit generalizability of the findings to more realistic, larger-scale software engineering optimization scenarios.

The paper's contribution is largely dataset construction plus an off-the-shelf refinement pipeline; the significance/impact for the broader field, beyond this specific benchmark setting, is somewhat narrow.

strengths: The core idea of shifting from single-programmer (user-oriented) optimization trajectories to problem-oriented trajectories that aggregate solutions from multiple programmers is intuitive and reasonably well-motivated with qualitative examples.

The paper backs its claim with a multi-dimensional analysis (Graph Edit Distance on CFGs, t-SNE semantic embedding dispersion, and human/LLM categorization of optimization types) that consistently supports the narrative that PCO pairs involve more global/algorithmic changes than PIE pairs.

The anchor verification idea, using the known-correct 'slow code' as an oracle to generate verified input/output test cases rather than relying on LLM-synthesized outputs, is a sensible and cheap way to reduce test-case-generation noise in the optimization-refinement setting.
Experiments span multiple model families and sizes (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4/4o, DeepSeek-V3) and both BEST@1/BEST@8 decoding, giving a reasonably broad empirical footprint.
Reasonable reproducibility support: prompts, training hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and code release are provided.
weaknesses: Potential confound in the PCO vs. PIE comparison: PCO pairs are constructed by sorting ALL valid submissions across all users by runtime and taking adjacent pairs, then keeping the 'top speedup' pairs per problem to match PIE's pair count. This selection procedure inherently biases PCO pairs toward much larger slow-to-fast runtime gaps (since it draws from the full cross-user runtime spectrum rather than each individual's incremental trajectory), which could mechanically inflate measured SPEEDUP/%OPT gains regardless of any genuine improvement in 'algorithmic' reasoning ability. The paper does not adequately control for or ablate this selection effect (e.g., by matching average speedup magnitude between PIE and PCO pairs), making it hard to disentangle 'problem-oriented diversity' from 'larger training deltas'.

The problem-oriented pairing procedure ('All users: [A1, C1, B1, A2, B3, C2, ..., CM]', taking consecutive pairs after globally sorting by runtime) can pair semantically and stylistically unrelated solutions (different data structures, even implicitly different algorithms unrelated to genuine 'improvement' narratives), and the paper provides no systematic analysis of how many such pairs are noisy/adversarial versus genuinely instructive, beyond a 100-sample human study.

Evaluation is restricted to a single narrow domain: competitive-programming C++ submissions from CodeNet judged via the gem5 simulator. No results are shown for other languages, real-world software repositories, or non-competitive-programming code, limiting claims of general applicability to 'code optimization' broadly.

Human and LLM sampling analyses (100 and 1,000 pairs, respectively) are relatively small for the strong categorical claims made (e.g., 78% vs 44% global optimization), and no inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals are reported.

No comparison against other plausible baselines for improving optimization capability besides the PIE dataset itself (e.g., data augmentation techniques, retrieval-based methods, or alternative curriculum/pairing strategies), making it unclear whether the improvement is specific to the proposed problem-oriented construction or could be achieved by simpler means such as filtering PIE pairs for larger speedup deltas.

Anchor verification's core assumption, that LLM-generated test inputs from a slow-code explanation adequately cover functional edge cases, is not rigorously validated (e.g., no coverage analysis against the original judge's hidden test suites); the method still leaves substantial residual incorrectness (~25-30%) after refinement, and the single-iteration cap used for all methods may not reflect their full potential, limiting the fairness of the comparison.

Results are reported as single-run point estimates without variance across seeds or multiple fine-tuning runs, so the magnitude of reported improvements cannot be judged against noise inherent to LLM fine-tuning and sampling.

The framing of 'first to introduce a problem-oriented perspective' is a fairly incremental data-curation contribution rather than a new modeling or algorithmic technique, and the paper's overall novelty is modest relative to the extensive empirical apparatus built around it.

strengths: The core idea—reconstructing optimization pairs from a problem-oriented (cross-programmer) perspective rather than a user-oriented (single-programmer iterative) perspective—is simple, well-motivated, and intuitively compelling for capturing algorithmic (global) rather than merely incremental (local) optimizations.

The multi-dimensional analysis (Control Flow Graph edit distance, semantic t-SNE embeddings, and human + LLM sampling of optimization types) provides converging quantitative and qualitative evidence that problem-oriented pairs indeed encode more diverse, structurally distinct optimizations than user-oriented pairs.

Extensive experiments across five different Code LLM backbones/sizes (CodeLlama 13B, DeepSeekCoder 7B/33B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/32B) and decoding strategies (BEST@1, BEST@8) consistently show large, non-trivial improvements in %OPT and SPEEDUP when switching from PIE to PCO fine-tuning data.

The anchor verification mechanism is a clever, low-overhead idea that exploits a unique property of the code optimization setting (the slow code is functionally correct and can act as an oracle for generating verified test cases), and it is benchmarked fairly against reasonable alternatives (self-debugging, direct test generation) across three different LLM backbones (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), showing consistent gains in correctness, %OPT, and speedup.

Useful ablations are included, such as the PCO data-percentage analysis showing that even 30% of PCO pairs outperform the full PIE dataset, supporting a data-efficiency claim, and application of anchor verification to the PIE baseline to further validate generality of the mechanism.
The paper is generally clearly written, with helpful figures (Fig. 1, 5, 6) and detailed case studies in the appendix that make the pipeline and failure modes concrete.
weaknesses: A central conceptual concern is not fully addressed: because problem-oriented pairs combine arbitrary slow code from one user with arbitrary fast code from a different user (potentially with an entirely different algorithmic structure/logic), a model fine-tuned on such pairs may effectively learn to disregard the input "slow" code and instead regenerate a good solution for the underlying problem from scratch, rather than truly "optimizing" the given code. The large GED/semantic-diversity results presented as a strength could equally be read as evidence that many pairs are only loosely related, which raises questions about whether the reported %OPT/SPEEDUP gains reflect genuine optimization capability versus disguised code-generation capability. This should have been more rigorously investigated (e.g., analyzing overlap/derivation relationships between the model's generated code and the specific slow input vs. the paired reference fast code).

Fine-tuning on PCO noticeably hurts CORRECT relative to PIE at BEST@1 in some cases and especially at BEST@8 (Finding 1), indicating a real correctness/optimization trade-off that anchor verification only partially closes; the residual correctness gap and its practical implications (e.g., silent incorrect "optimizations" in deployment) deserve more discussion.

Evaluation is confined to a single domain (competitive-programming C++ code from CodeNet/PIE) and a single optimization objective (execution time under gem5 simulation with -O3). Generalization to real-world software repositories, other languages, or other optimization goals (memory, energy) is untested, despite the paper's broader framing of "code optimization."

The construction of PCO retains only the same number of pairs per problem as PIE, selecting the top-speedup-ranked ones; this curation choice is not deeply justified or ablated, and could introduce selection bias favoring examples that are easiest to demonstrate large gains on.

Human and LLM sampling analyses (Section 3.2, Fig. 4 and 7) that support the core structural claims are based on small samples (100 pairs for human evaluation), and inter-annotator agreement or evaluation protocol details are not reported, limiting confidence in the categorical breakdowns.

The anchor verification framework introduces additional inference-time cost (multiple LLM calls for explanation, test generation, execution, and iterative refinement) which is not quantified or compared in terms of latency/cost trade-offs against the reported performance gains.

Baselines for the anchor verification comparison (self-debugging, direct test generation) are reasonable but relatively simple; comparison against more sophisticated verification/refinement techniques used in the code generation literature (e.g., iterative multi-round self-repair, majority voting across candidate test suites) is missing, making it harder to gauge how much of the anchor verification's advantage is due to the anchor idea specifically versus general iterative refinement.

strengths: Identifies a real and practically important gap: reconstructing optimization pairs from a problem-oriented perspective (aggregating multiple programmers' solutions to the same problem) rather than the standard user-oriented (single-programmer trajectory) approach used in prior work (PIE).

Very thorough multi-dimensional empirical validation of the problem-oriented hypothesis: structural analysis via Graph Edit Distance, semantic embedding/t-SNE analysis, and both human and LLM categorization of optimization types (global vs. local), all consistently supporting the claim that problem-oriented pairs capture more diverse/global algorithmic changes.

Careful ablation studies that disentangle the perspective effect from the selection (top-speedup sampling) effect (PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup vs. PIE), and GED-stratified fine-tuning experiments, which strengthen the causal claims about why the problem-oriented approach works.

Large-scale, consistent gains across multiple model families and scales (CodeLlama, DeepSeekCoder 7B/33B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/32B) and across BEST@1/BEST@8 decoding, as well as a well-motivated 'anchor verification' framework that meaningfully improves correctness, %OPT, and speedup over self-debugging and direct test-generation baselines across three different LLM backbones.

Extensive supplementary validation: cross-language replication on Python, physical hardware validation against gem5 simulation results, cost/practical-overhead analysis, iteration-count ablation, and detailed qualitative case studies, which collectively bolster reproducibility and practical relevance.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat limited: the problem-oriented perspective is essentially a data-reordering/curation trick (sorting all cross-user submissions by runtime and pairing sequentially), and the anchor verification framework is an incremental adaptation of existing execution-feedback/test-case-generation refinement techniques (e.g., CodeT, Self-Debug) to the optimization setting.

Test-case-based correctness verification (both for the main %CORRECT metric and within the anchor framework) can still miss edge cases; the anchor framework's effectiveness is bounded by the quality/coverage of LLM-generated test inputs, which is not deeply analyzed beyond a single ablation (Table 3).

No comparison against alternative or more recent code-optimization-specific baselines beyond self-debugging and direct test generation (e.g., retrieval-augmented approaches, RL-based optimization, or other established performance-improving code-edit methods), leaving the relative positioning against the broader literature underexplored.

Much of the critical validation (cross-language generalization, hardware validation, cost analysis, failure-mode analysis) is relegated to appendices rather than integrated into the main paper, and some experiments (e.g., 20-sample physical hardware validation) are fairly small-scale.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported for the main results, despite BEST@k sampling introducing stochasticity, making it hard to assess the robustness of the reported percentage-point improvements.

The paper's framing of contributions (e.g., 'first to introduce a problem-oriented perspective') is a strong claim for what is fundamentally a dataset-construction strategy; the significance of the contribution to the broader field beyond this specific optimization-pair benchmark is somewhat narrow.

strengths: The core empirical claim -- that pooling solutions from many programmers for the same problem yields richer, more 'global' optimization supervision than single-user iterative trajectories -- is intuitive and is backed by multiple complementary analyses (Graph Edit Distance, t-SNE semantic clustering, human and LLM categorization of edit type).

Extensive experimental coverage: five LLM backbones/sizes, BEST@1/BEST@8 decoding, data-scarcity/percentage ablations, a controlled study that disentangles the 'perspective' effect from the 'top-speedup selection' effect (Appendix H), GED-stratified subset ablations, cross-language (Python) replication, and even physical-hardware validation against gem5 simulation.

The anchor verification framework is a sensible, low-overhead idea: using the known-correct-but-slow code as an oracle to generate verified I/O test cases, rather than relying on LLM-synthesized outputs that can themselves be wrong. The 'Comparison Group' ablation (using LLM-guessed outputs instead of real execution) nicely isolates why real execution matters.
Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations, failure-mode breakdown (Appendix I), iteration-count studies, and cost/latency analysis of the proposed refinement pipeline.
Solid engineering documentation (training details, prompts, GPU hours) that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual validity concern with the 'problem-oriented pair' construction: pairing two independently-written correct solutions from different users, sorted only by runtime (e.g., (A1,C1),(C1,B1)), does not represent a genuine edit/optimization trajectory the way a single user's iterative refinement does. The model is trained to treat two unrelated programs as if one were derived by 'optimizing' the other, which is a questionable supervision signal even if it empirically improves benchmark numbers; this construct-validity issue is not seriously interrogated beyond showing that performance improves.

The magnitude of gains (e.g., %OPT 31%→59%, speedup 2.95×→5.22×) is very large for what is essentially a data-reorganization trick, raising the concern that the model may be learning to recognize problem-specific algorithmic tricks common in competitive programming (prefix sums, hashing, DP-state reduction) rather than a generalizable 'code optimization' skill -- i.e., possible overfitting to the narrow distribution of CodeNet/competitive-programming idioms rather than genuine algorithmic reasoning transferable to real software.

All experiments are conducted on competitive-programming benchmarks (CodeNet-derived PIE/PCO); the 'Discussion of Generalizability to Complex Real-World Scenarios' in Sec. 4 is purely speculative/qualitative and not empirically tested, so claims about real-world software optimization applicability are unsupported.
The test set is small (41 unique problems, 978 pairs), limiting the statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially the fine-grained per-metric deltas in Tables 2-4.

Novelty of the anchor verification framework is incremental relative to existing execution-feedback/self-repair literature (CodeT, Self-Debug, LDB); the core difference (use the slow code, not synthesized tests, as the oracle) is a reasonable but fairly narrow technical contribution.

At BEST@8, correctness for PCO-tuned models is sometimes worse than for PIE-tuned models (Finding 1), indicating the proposed perspective trades off correctness for aggressive optimization in some regimes; this trade-off is acknowledged but not fully resolved.

Human and LLM categorization studies (global/local/other) rely on small samples (100 pairs) and subjective category boundaries, weakening the strength of the qualitative claims about 'algorithmic innovation'.

The paper's writing is dense with contributions spread thinly across a large appendix; several important robustness results (disentangling ablation, GED-stratified ablation, hardware validation) are relegated to appendices rather than being core to the main narrative, making it harder to assess the paper's true robustness from the main text alone.

strengths: The problem-oriented perspective is a simple, well-motivated reframing of the code optimization pair construction problem, and the paper provides convincing multi-dimensional evidence (Graph Edit Distance structural analysis, t-SNE semantic embedding analysis, and both human and LLM-based categorization of optimization types) that PCO pairs capture more global/algorithmic changes than the PIE user-oriented pairs.

Extensive fine-tuning experiments across a wide range of model families and sizes (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4/4o, DeepSeek-V3) consistently show large and reproducible gains in %OPT, SPEEDUP and CORRECT for PCO over PIE, at both BEST@1 and BEST@8.

Careful ablations disentangle the contribution of the problem-oriented perspective from the top-speedup selection strategy (PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup vs. PIE), which strengthens the causal claim that the perspective itself (not just curation) drives the gains.

The anchor verification framework is a well-motivated, domain-specific innovation that exploits the unique property of code optimization (the slow code is functionally correct) to produce verified test cases, and is rigorously compared against reasonable baselines (self-debugging, direct test generation) with a 'root cause' ablation isolating the effect of accurate vs. LLM-hallucinated test outputs.

Broad generalizability checks are included: cross-language validation on Python, validation on physical hardware (vs. gem5 simulation only), scaling/iteration analyses, cost-benefit analysis of BEST@k, GED-stratified fine-tuning ablations, and a systematic failure-mode breakdown, all of which substantially strengthen the empirical case and preemptively address likely concerns.

The paper is transparent about limitations (remaining correctness gap, scope limited to execution-time optimization) and provides detailed reproducibility information (training configs, prompts, GPU hours).
weaknesses: The core PCO pairing mechanically pairs code from different, unrelated authors purely by runtime rank; unlike PIE's within-user edits, these pairs are not true 'edits' but heterogeneous slow/fast program pairs for the same problem, which raises the question of whether SFT on PCO teaches genuine 'optimization' transformations versus simply conditioning the model to reproduce a known efficient solution for that problem (memorization/lookup risk), especially given competitive-programming datasets often contain many structurally similar problems.

The claim that PCO teaches transferable 'edit patterns' (Appendix O) rests on a single qualitative case study rather than systematic quantitative evidence, which is weak support for a fairly strong generalization claim.

The anchor verification framework's Stage 1 (test input generation) still relies entirely on the LLM's understanding of the slow code; if the LLM misunderstands the code's semantics or misses edge cases, the anchoring of outputs does not compensate for poor/incomplete input coverage, so correctness gains, while real, are bounded by this dependency.

Reliance on relatively small val/test splits (2,544 / 978 pairs from 77/41 unique problems) for a competitive-programming domain leaves some uncertainty about robustness/variance of the reported percentage-point improvements.

Overall novelty of the problem-oriented perspective is somewhat incremental relative to PIE (essentially aggregating and re-sorting existing submissions rather than a fundamentally new data collection methodology), though the empirical execution and analysis are thorough.

Some important validation results (Python generalizability, hardware validation, failure analysis, cost-benefit) are relegated entirely to the appendix, making the main paper somewhat less self-contained.
